title: 01. The lexicon: what "aliveness" means, and how that changed
md:
**Question.** Which words carried what we now call aliveness, and was life a
substance, a principle, a breath, a heat, an activity or a relation? ◐ claims are marked; ○ claims are not cited.

## Opening

No tradition in this knowledge base has a single word for aliveness. The English noun for a felt quality
reaches Source Library's pages only through New Thought writers around 1900 [[1]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-mod-aliveness-is-a-new-thought-word).
The older words answer different questions. *What lives?* Aristotle answers with verbs: life is said "in many
ways", and a thing lives if it nourishes itself, grows, senses or moves [[2]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-deanima-ensouled-distinguished-by-living).
*What moves?* Thales, as Aristotle reports him, gave the magnet a soul because it moves iron [[3]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-thales-magnet-has-soul).
*What breathes?* Tertullian: to breathe is to live, and not to breathe is not to live [[4]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-tertullian-to-breathe-is-to-live).
*What heals and lasts?* Caraka's word āyus is lifespan, the union of body, senses, mind and self
[[5]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-caraka-ayus-union-definition). Breath in Genesis 2:7 is the breath *of* life, not life itself
[[6]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-breath-of-life-is-not-life).

The conceptions behind the words fall into about eleven kinds, and the same culture usually held several at
once [[7]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-wil-no-era-has-one-definition). Life as a **substance**: ojas, the quintessence, mumia
[[8]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-ojas-sushruta) [[9]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/alchemy-medicine#alch-rupescissa-quintessence-heaven-of-human-body) [[10]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/alchemy-medicine#wil-paracelsus-life-is-balsamic-mummy).
A **principle**: Aristotle's soul as the first entelechy of an organic body [[11]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-deanima-soul-first-entelechy-organic-body).
A **breath**: prāṇa, rlung, ruach [[12]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-hyp-life-is-breath-staying) [[13]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-rlung-rendered-wind) [[14]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-ezekiel37-one-ruach-three-englishes).
A **heat**: the innate heat of the heart [[15]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil-aristotle-living-warm-dead-cold). A **moisture**: the radical
moisture that heat feeds on [[16]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-bacon-heat-consumes-its-own-oil). A **soul** spread through the world
[[17]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-agrippa-absurd-that-world-not-live). A **force**: Lebenskraft [[18]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-wenzel-1800-life-gradual-dying).
An **activity**: Bichat's functions that resist death [[19]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-bichat-1800-ensemble-des-fonctions). An
**organization**: Kant's product in which everything is end and means [[20]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil-kant-organized-product-end-and-means).
A **relation** or state: qi gathered [[21]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-zhuangzi-life-gathering-of-qi) [[22]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-asia-life-is-a-state-not-a-stuff).
A **mechanism**: Hobbes's "motion of Limbs" [[23]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-hobbes-life-is-motion-of-limbs).

That is 43 terms. Three patterns show in it. The ancient Mediterranean words name a breath or a heat
that *serves* life rather than being it [[6]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-breath-of-life-is-not-life) [[127]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-med-heat-moisture-is-instrument-not-definition).
The Chinese, Sanskrit and Tibetan definitions are positional or relational: qi gathered, vāyu staying, a union
of four [[22]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-asia-life-is-a-state-not-a-stuff). And the words for a *force* of life (Lebenskraft, principe
vital, libido) arrive after 1790 [[18]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-wenzel-1800-life-gradual-dying) [[85]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-kardec-1857-principe-vital-effect-and-cause) [[91]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-jung-libido-energy-of-life-process-1921).

## Definitions of life, era by era

Each line is marked by what it defines life through: what life **DOES**, what a living thing **HAS**, or
what life **IS PART OF**. The spine is a convenience; no era had one definition [[7]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-wil-no-era-has-one-definition).

- **6th c. BCE, Anaximenes.** "As our soul, being air, holds us together, so do breath and air encompass the whole world." IS PART OF [[27]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-anaximenes-soul-air-holds-us-together).
- **4th–3rd c. BCE, Zhuangzi.** "Human life is the gathering of qi. When it gathers, there is life; when it disperses, there is death." IS PART OF (one qi) [[21]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-zhuangzi-life-gathering-of-qi).
- **c. 350 BCE, Aristotle.** "By life we mean self-sustained nutrition, growth, and decay." DOES [[24]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-deanima-life-is-self-nourishment-growth-decay). And elsewhere: "life is the maintenance of this heat." HAS [[128]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil-aristotle-life-is-maintenance-of-heat).
- **c. 90–110 CE, John.** "In him was life, and the life was the light of men." IS PART OF [[129]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-john-1-4-life-in-the-logos).
- **Early centuries CE, Caraka.** "The combination of the body, senses, mind, and soul is called life." IS PART OF (a union) [[5]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-caraka-ayus-union-definition).
- **c. 210, Tertullian.** "Quid est … spirare: flatum … ex semetipso agere. Quid est non uiuere: flatum … ex semetipso non agere." DOES [[4]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-tertullian-to-breathe-is-to-live).
- **2nd–3rd c., Corpus Hermeticum XII.** The cosmos "πλήρωμα ἐστὶ τῆς πάσης ζωῆς", the fullness of all life, and nothing in it is dead. IS PART OF [[130]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-hermetica-cosmos-pleroma-of-life-nothing-dead).
- **c. 250, Plotinus.** "Omnis vita est intelligentia quaedam", every life is a kind of thought. IS PART OF [[131]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-plotinus-every-life-is-a-kind-of-thought).
- **c. 1268, Aquinas.** "Those are properly living things which move themselves." DOES [[132]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-aquinas-living-things-move-themselves).
- **c. 1310, Pietro d'Abano.** "Vita est processio procedens ab ente sempiterno quieto." IS PART OF [[133]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil-abano-life-procession-from-being). On other pages heat and moisture are its formal causes: HAS [[134]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil-abano-heat-moisture-essential-cause).
- **15th c., Haṭhayogapradīpikā.** "As long as the breath remains in the body, it is called life. Its departure is death." HAS [[12]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-hyp-life-is-breath-staying).
- **c. 1527, Paracelsus.** "Life is nothing else but a certain Balsamic Mummy." HAS [[10]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/alchemy-medicine#wil-paracelsus-life-is-balsamic-mummy).
- **1623, Francis Bacon.** The vital spirit is "whole and exists independently", continuous through channels. HAS [[135]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#wil-bacon-vital-spirit-whole-and-self-standing) [[136]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#wil-bacon-vital-spirit-continuous-channels).
- **1634, Cremonini.** "If life consists in heat and moisture … every living thing is of a hot and moist complexion." HAS [[137]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#wil-cremonini-life-consists-in-heat-moisture).
- **1648, van Helmont.** "Vita est lumen & initium formale, quo res agit, quod agere jussa est." IS PART OF (a created order) [[138]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/alchemy-medicine#wil-helmont-life-is-light-formal-beginning).
- **1651, Hobbes.** "Life is but a motion of Limbs." DOES [[23]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-hobbes-life-is-motion-of-limbs). **1651, Harvey:** "the life, therefore, resides in the blood." HAS [[139]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-harvey-life-resides-in-blood).
- **1666, Cavendish.** "Motion is the life and soul of Nature." IS PART OF [[140]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-cavendish-motion-life-and-soul-of-nature). **1690, Conway:** God "made no dead thing." IS PART OF [[141]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-conway-god-made-no-dead-thing).
- **1790, Kant.** "An organized product of nature is one in which everything is an end and, reciprocally, also a means." DOES (organizes); Kant calls it only an "analogue of life" [[20]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil-kant-organized-product-end-and-means) [[142]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil-kant-organism-formative-power-not-machine).
- **1798–99, Schelling.** Life comes about "invita natura externa", against the will of external nature. DOES [[143]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-schelling-1799-life-against-external-nature). Its principle links all nature into one organism: IS PART OF [[86]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-schelling-1798-world-soul-universal-organism).
- **1800, Bichat.** "La vie est l'ensemble des fonctions qui résistent à la mort." DOES [[19]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-bichat-1800-ensemble-des-fonctions).
- **1857, Kardec.** "La vie est un effet produit par l'action d'un agent sur la matière." HAS (an agent) [[85]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-kardec-1857-principe-vital-effect-and-cause).
- **1868, Huxley.** "Protoplasm … is the formal basis of all life." HAS [[144]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-huxley-1868-protoplasm-formal-basis).
- **1907, Bergson.** "La vie est, avant tout, une tendance à agir sur la matière brute." DOES [[89]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-bergson-life-tendency-to-act-on-matter-1907).
- **1912, Patterson (New Thought).** "The man who is truly alive is the man who is conscious of his oneness with the Divine Life." IS PART OF [[145]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-patterson-truly-alive-oneness-1912).
- **1921, Jung.** Libido is "nothing other than the energy of the life-process." HAS [[91]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-jung-libido-energy-of-life-process-1921).
- **1929, Whitehead.** "Life is a bid for freedom." DOES [[146]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil-whitehead-life-bid-for-freedom).

Read down the marks and the shift is not one-way. DOES opens with Aristotle and Tertullian and returns with
Aquinas, Hobbes, Bichat and Bergson. HAS clusters in the medical centuries (heat, moisture, spirit, blood,
balsam, protoplasm). IS PART OF runs alongside both, from Heraclitus through Cavendish and Schelling to New
Thought. Mechanist and animist in the 1650s–60s gave the same answer, motion [[147]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-ems-motion-is-life-on-both-sides).
After 1818 a second question joins the first: the life one lives and values, not the living body
(Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Dilthey), which is the old split between bios and zōē
[[148]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-wil-zoe-and-bios-conflated) [[149]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#wil-schopenhauer-life-mirror-of-will) [[150]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil-nietzsche-life-is-will-to-power).

## What life is, philosopher by philosopher

A second reading of the philosophers asked one question: what does each say life IS? One line per thinker,
marked as above (DOES / HAS / IS PART OF), quoting SL's English unless the original is given. All ✓ verified on
the page except the Neiye (◐, snippet only). Where the list above already holds a thinker's line it is not repeated.

**Greek and Roman**
- **c. 500 BCE, Heraclitus.** Soul is a phase in the cycle of the elements: "To souls it is death to become water … and from water, soul." IS PART OF [[151]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-heraclitus-souls-death-to-become-water). "We live their death and they live our death." [[152]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-heraclitus-we-live-their-death)
- **c. 450 BCE, Empedocles.** "πάντα γὰρ ἴσθι φρόνησιν ἔχειν καὶ νώματος αἶσαν" (Leonard: "All things have fixed intent and share of thought"). HAS, and everything has it [[153]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-empedocles-all-things-have-thought). He also promises "every drug … made defense 'gainst sickness and old age" [[154]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-empedocles-drugs-against-old-age).
- **c. 380 BCE, Plato, *Phaedo*.** What makes a body alive? "The soul … if the soul takes possession of anything it always brings life to it" (ἀεὶ ἥκει … φέρουσα ζωήν). HAS [[155]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-plato-phaedo-soul-brings-life).
- **c. 370 BCE, Plato, *Phaedrus*.** "that which has its motion within itself has a soul" (ἔνδοθεν αὐτῷ ἐξ αὑτοῦ, ἔμψυχον). DOES [[156]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-plato-phaedrus-self-mover-is-soul).
- **c. 350 BCE, Plato, *Laws* X.** A thing that moves itself is to be called alive, and soul's definition is "the motion able to move itself". DOES [[157]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-plato-laws-x-self-motion-is-alive).
- **3rd c. BCE, the Stoics (SVF II.1013).** Things are held together in three grades, "ἕξεως μὲν ὡς λίθοι καὶ ξύλα, φύσεως δὲ καθάπερ τὰ φυτά, ψυχῆς δὲ τὰ ζῶα" (stones by hexis, plants by physis, animals by psychē), and the world, a sympathetic unified body, is held by soul. IS PART OF [[158]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-stoic-cosmos-held-by-soul-not-hexis).
- **45 BCE, Cicero.** "sapientem esse mundum necesse est": the world must be wise, and so a god. IS PART OF [[159]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-cicero-nd-world-is-wise-and-god).
- **c. 55 BCE, Lucretius.** The mind is "extremely fine and consists of exceedingly minute bodies": life with no principle but small, fast atoms. HAS [[160]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-lucretius-mind-made-of-minute-bodies).
- **c. 180 CE, Galen.** Attraction, retention, alteration and excretion, "the handmaids of nutrition", belong to every nourished part. DOES [[161]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-galen-nf-four-faculties-handmaids-of-nutrition).

**Late antique, Jewish, Islamic, Indic and Chinese**
- **c. 40 CE, Philo, *Questions on Genesis*.** The moulded man "obtained a soul by God breathing life into his face", a mixture of the corruptible and the incorruptible. HAS (by gift) [[162]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#wil2-philo-qg-life-breathed-into-face).
- **Early centuries CE, Caraka (Kaviratna 1890).** "The union of body, senses, mind, and soul is called Life"; mind, soul and body rest "on union like three sticks". IS PART OF [[163]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#wil2-caraka-kaviratna-union-called-life) [[164]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#wil2-caraka-tridanda-person-rests-on-union).

- **c. 4th c. BCE, Guanzi "Neiye" (◐).** "氣道乃生 … 生乃思": when qi flows there is life; with life, thought. DOES [[167]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#wil2-neiye-qi-flows-then-life-then-thought).
- **139 BCE, Huainanzi.** "生生者未嘗死也其所生則死矣": what gives life to life has never died; only what it produced dies. IS PART OF [[168]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#wil2-huainanzi-what-gives-life-to-life-never-dies) (SL's English says "vital energy" for 氣: tagged `mistranslation`).
- **Early 11th c., Avicenna, *Compendium de anima*.** "a living body … is distinguished from a non-living body by its soul, and not by its body." HAS [[169]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-avicenna-living-body-differs-by-soul-first-perfection).
- **c. 1050, Ibn Gabirol, *Fons vitae*.** The fruit of philosophy: "Euasio mortis et applicatio ad originem uitae", escape from death and attachment to the origin of life. IS PART OF [[170]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-gabirol-fruit-escape-death-origin-of-life).
- **c. 1175, Ibn Tufayl, *Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān*.** Hayy opens the dead doe's heart and finds the left cavity "empty, containing nothing" (خال لاشي فيه): "my object was in it, then it departed and left it vacant." In a living animal the cavity holds a burning white vapour, and "this moist vapor was what had moved this animal"; through that one spirit (الروح) each animal is one. HAS, in one place, and can lose it whole [[171]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-opens-the-doe-seeking-the-seat) [[172]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-what-left-was-the-mother) [[173]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-vivisection-hot-vapour-moved-animal) [[174]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-animal-one-through-its-spirit).

**Early modern**

DOES, and every thing does it, not only the living [[175]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-spinoza-each-thing-strives-to-persevere) [[176]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-spinoza-conatus-is-actual-essence). - **1714, Leibniz, *Monadology*.** "What we call births are developments and unfoldings, and what we call deaths are foldings and shrinkages." IS PART OF (a life never begun or ended) [[179]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-leibniz-no-birth-no-death-unfolding) [[180]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-leibniz-metamorphosis-not-metempsychosis) [[181]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-leibniz-preformation-from-seeds). - **1748, La Mettrie.** "L'organiſation ſuffiroit-elle donc à tout? oüi, encore une fois." - **1749, Buffon (as Dutens reports him, 1796).** A matter "composée de particules organiques toujours actives, tendantes sans cesse à l'organisation". HAS (a living stuff) [[187]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil2-buffon-organic-particles-dutens) [[188]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil2-biran-buffon-vital-coordination).
- **1790, Goethe.** "the laws of transformation by which nature produces one part through another". DOES [[189]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#wil2-goethe-1790-laws-of-transformation).
- **1769, Diderot, *Le rêve de d'Alembert*.** Held but not yet transcribed.

**Modern**
- **1818, Schopenhauer.** "das Leben unsers Leibes nur ein fortdauernd gehemmtes Sterben, ein immer aufgeschobener Tod ist": the body's life is a continually checked dying. DOES (against death) [[190]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-schopenhauer-life-inhibited-dying).

IS PART OF [[191]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-butler-mechanical-consciousness) [[192]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-butler-vapour-engine-feeds) [[193]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-butler-man-in-machine-reproduction).
- **1883, Dilthey.** Society and history are built from "Lebenseinheiten, den psychophysischen Individuis", each of them "eine Welt". IS PART OF [[194]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-dilthey-lebenseinheiten).
- **1887–88, Nietzsche (Nachlass).** Values are "nur ein Symptom von Kraft … eine Simplifikation zum Zweck des Lebens". DOES [[195]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-nietzsche-values-symptom-for-life) (SL's English says "power" for *Kraft*: tagged `mistranslation`).
- **1906–7, William James.** "Everyone is familiar with the phenomenon of feeling more or less alive on different days." "Compared with what we ought to be, we are only half awake." HAS, in degrees [[196]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-james-feeling-more-or-less-alive). "our organism has stored-up reserves of energy that are ordinarily not called upon" [[197]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-james-second-wind-reserves); "Excitements, ideas, and efforts … are what carry us over the dam" [[198]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-james-excitements-ideas-efforts) [[199]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-james-energizing-qualitative-level).
- **1907, Bergson.** "la vie tout entière … apparaît comme un effort pour accumuler de l'énergie et pour la lâcher ensuite". DOES [[200]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil2-bergson-life-store-and-spend-energy).
- **1913–16, Scheler.** Vital values are felt in "alle Modi des Lebensgefühls (z. B. das Gefühl des »aufsteigenden« und des »niedergehenden« Lebens …)". HAS (as a feeling) [[201]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-scheler-vital-values-noble-common).

What the second reading adds. Self-motion, not breath, is the first Greek *definition* of life (Plato, before
Aristotle). Spinoza takes life's oldest mark, self-preservation, and gives it to every thing. Hayy makes the
seat of life something one looks for with a knife. And by 1872 the question can be put to a steam engine.

Three findings. First, most of it lives in the gloss and note layer, not the running text: the running
translation often has the narrow word ("breath of life", "wind") and a gloss adds "life force"; in the
Gheranda the gloss is added to a page that was already English [[215]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-cmp-life-force-is-a-gloss-layer)
[[109]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-shengqi-jingyue-shenqi) [[13]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-rlung-rendered-wind). Second, the same habit names Renaissance terms
with 19th-century vitalist words, so a count of "vital force" over SL's English finds the concept earlier than
the texts do [[216]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-ren-vital-force-glosses). Third, "prāṇa = energy" has a print date: Yogi Ramacharaka
(W. W. Atkinson) calls prāṇa "the Sanskrit term meaning 'Absolute Energy'" in Chicago in 1905
[[217]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-ramacharaka-prana-absolute-energy), while the Haṭhayogapradīpikā's commentator glosses prāṇa as vāyu,
wind, and Müller in 1879 rendered it "breath" [[218]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-asia-energy-gloss-has-a-date). The English phrase itself
is at home in mind-cure and Theosophy around 1900: Evans in 1881, Steiner's "life-force … called Prana" in 1904,
Atkinson's "Asserting the Life-Force" in 1906 [[219]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-evans-life-spiritual-force-not-fluid-1881)
[[220]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-steiner-life-force-is-prana-1904) [[221]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-atkinson-put-life-into-you-1906).

Not every case is a gloss on a single word. Scripture splits one word into two Englishes: ruach is "breath"
in Ezekiel 37:5–8 and "spirit" in 9–10, and Psalm 104's one πνεῦμα becomes "breath" then "spirit"
[[14]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-ezekiel37-one-ruach-three-englishes) [[222]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-psalm104-lxx-one-pneuma-two-englishes). In 1 Cor 15:45
"a living soul" becomes "a living being", so the soul drops out [[42]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-1cor15-psyche-zosa-pneuma-zoopoioun).
The reverse also happens: Fechner's "lebendige Kraft" (vis viva, literally "living force") becomes "kinetic
energy", physically fair but anachronistic for 1851, and the word "living" disappears just where Fechner joins
mechanics to soul [[223]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-fechner-1851-lebendige-kraft-kinetic-energy). One case, in a c. 1280 Canon
manuscript, is only ◐ partial: the scan may read "ratione vitae", not a force [[224]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-avicenna-canon-ms-life-force).

## Critiques

- **Against reading the words as one thing.** Breath conditions life and is not life [[6]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-breath-of-life-is-not-life); the translator, not the Hebrew, chooses breath or spirit [[225]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-heb-breath-or-spirit-is-the-translators-choice); qi and prāṇa name a state, not a stuff [[22]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-asia-life-is-a-state-not-a-stuff), and what they share is breath, not energy [[226]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-cmp-breath-energy-pairing); ming is allotted life [disputed]; mana, orenda and manitou were made one force by the glosses [disputed] [[227]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anim-aston-spiritual-being-too-narrow).
- **Against reading the past through later vitalism.** Aristotle's soul is no agent [[228]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-entelechy-is-not-an-agent); heat and moisture are the soul's instrument [[127]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-med-heat-moisture-is-instrument-not-definition); light is a theory of body [[229]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-med-light-is-not-life); "molecular" āyus is a back-projection [[230]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-asia-molecular-ayus-backprojection); the five soul-levels are late [[231]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-heb-five-soul-levels-are-late); the elixir preserves rather than adds life [[232]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-alch-elixir-preserves-rather-than-vivifies).
- **Against tidy doctrines.** The living cosmos was contested [[233]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-living-world-was-contested) [[234]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-thales-is-aristotles-reconstruction), as were the life of metals [[235]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-alch-life-of-metals-metaphor-or-doctrine), Renaissance panpsychism [[71]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-ren-panpsychism-not-one-world-soul) and the Romantic living Earth [[87]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-rom-living-earth-not-shared) [[236]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-rom-naturphilosophie-not-lebenskraft-vitalism).
- **Against the mechanism-versus-vitalism story.** Both sides defined life as motion [[147]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-ems-motion-is-life-on-both-sides); "dead matter" is the critics' word [[237]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-vit-dead-matter-is-the-critics-word); the binary is retrospective [[238]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-vit-binary-retrospective) [[239]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-vit-irritability-served-both-sides); the critics killed the word, not the definition [[240]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-vit-killed-word-kept-definition).
- **Against the modern end of the table.** "Aliveness" is a New Thought word [[1]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-mod-aliveness-is-a-new-thought-word); libido-as-energy has no measure [[241]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-mod-libido-energy-has-no-measure); no era has one definition, and Schopenhauer's or Dilthey's "life" answers a different question from Aristotle's [[7]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-wil-no-era-has-one-definition) [[148]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-wil-zoe-and-bios-conflated).

## Open questions

1. When does English "life force" first appear in print as a noun, and through whom? The earliest on SL's pages so far is mind-cure (Evans 1881) [[219]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-evans-life-spiritual-force-not-fluid-1881); the vitalist translators of Lebenskraft are not yet checked.
2. Is there a pre-modern word anywhere in the corpus that means a *felt* aliveness, as Wilmans's noun does [[93]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-wilmans-aliveness-childhood-1898)? Candidates not yet read: thymos, Ficino's spiritus refreshed by green and odours [[242]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-ficino-green-holds-vernal-moisture).
3. The Chinese rows lean on ◐ claims for jing, shen and shengsheng [[108]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-neiye-jing-of-things-is-life) [[110]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-leishuo-qi-mother-of-shen) [[114]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-yijing-shengsheng-zhangzai); these need pages fetched before they can carry weight.
4. The Fernel definition ("maker and bond of life") is ◐ [[243]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-fernel-innate-spirit-maker-and-bond-of-life); a verified page would fill the 1548 gap in the spine.
5. How much of the "life force" layer is in SL's notes across the whole corpus, not just these pages? A count over glosses versus running text would turn the finding into a number [[215]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-cmp-life-force-is-a-gloss-layer).
6. Arabic beyond Avicenna and al-Ghazālī (ḥayāh, nafs) and the Tibetan bla are thin; mana and manitou reach us only through European ethnographers [[244]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/animism-ethnography#anim-doutte-mana-orenda-manitou-breath).

title: 2. Turning points: where the meaning of aliveness changed
md:
**The question.** Which moments in history changed what
aliveness meant? This page names ten. Each gives a date range, what changed (before → after), one to three
quotes copied from Source Library pages with the claim id and the page's shortlink, and the strongest standing
critique against it.

**How to read it.** Quotes are SL's English unless the original is given. Every claim cited here is ✓ verified
unless marked ◐. A turning point is where a new answer to "what makes a thing alive?" first appears on our pages.
It does not mean the old answer died. Most of these answers ran on side by side for centuries
[[1]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-wil-no-era-has-one-definition).

---

## 1. Breath becomes soul (6th c. BCE – c. 210 CE)

**Before → after.** Before this, the words were words for moving air. After it, they named what keeps a body
together and alive. Brinton (late 19th c.) says psychē, pneuma and thymos all come from roots for the motion of
wind or breath, and that one Hebrew word, ruach, is translated now as wind, now as spirit, now as breath
[[2]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-brinton-psyche-pneuma-thymos-from-wind). That is an interpretive claim. The texts show the move
directly. For Anaximenes, soul *is* air, and its work is holding us together, the same work breath does for the
cosmos [[3]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-anaximenes-soul-air-holds-us-together). In Genesis 2:7, God blows the "breath of life" (נשמת חיים)
into Adam, and the man becomes a "living nefesh" [[4]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-gen27-nishmat-hayyim-nefesh-hayyah). The Septuagint, as
Philo quotes it, renders that breath as πνοή (pnoē), not πνεῦμα, and nefesh as ψυχή
[[5]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-gen27-lxx-pnoe-not-pneuma). So the Greek Bible's breath of life is not yet the "spirit" of later theology.
By about 210, Tertullian defines living as breathing [[6]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-tertullian-to-breathe-is-to-live).

> "Just as our soul," he says, "being air, holds us together, so do breath and air encompass the whole world."
> [[3]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-anaximenes-soul-air-holds-us-together) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bl4pQvqHtpd92ful2DP

> Ἐνεφύσησεν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ πνοὴν ζωῆς, καὶ ἐγένετο ὁ ἄνθρωπος εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. ("He breathed into his
> face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.") [[5]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-gen27-lxx-pnoe-not-pneuma)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgV77qIFgtU0Iyz0iE1

> "What is it not to live? It is, I believe, not to drive breath from within oneself."
> [[6]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-tertullian-to-breathe-is-to-live) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhK94js5iwV2Lp3ptod

**Elsewhere.** India made the same move on its own. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad calls breath "the oldest and the
best" [[7]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-chandogya-breath-oldest-best). Much later, the Haṭhayogapradīpikā (15th c.) defines life as the
breath staying in the body: "As long as the breath remains in the body, it is called life. Its departure is
death." [[8]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-hyp-life-is-breath-staying) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BjlvoTqfGdnZcB6QepG

**Against this:** [[9]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-breath-of-life-is-not-life). On these pages breath is the carrier or condition of
life ("breath OF life"), not life itself. Also [[10]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-heb-breath-or-spirit-is-the-translators-choice): whether
ruach is "breath" or "spirit" is often the translator's choice.

## 2. Aristotle defines life by what a body does (c. 350 BCE)

**Before → after.** Before Aristotle, the earliest Greek test for having a soul was moving oneself: Thales's
magnet has a soul because it moves iron [[11]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-thales-magnet-has-soul). Plato turned the test into a
definition of soul: a body moved from within is ἔμψυχον, and soul is "the motion able to move itself"
[[12]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-plato-phaedrus-self-mover-is-soul) [[13]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-plato-laws-x-self-motion-is-alive). Soul is then what
"always brings life" to whatever it takes hold of [[14]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil2-plato-phaedo-soul-brings-life). Self-motion as the
mark of the living outlasts this turn: Aquinas still uses it [[15]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-aquinas-living-things-move-themselves).
Aristotle replaced the test with a definition of life itself, and he gave two. In *De anima*, life is an activity: a body's own nourishing, growing and decaying
[[16]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-deanima-life-is-self-nourishment-growth-decay). "Living" is said in many ways
[[17]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-deanima-ensouled-distinguished-by-living). In the short biological works, life is a state of heat: birth
is the nutritive soul's first share in heat, and life is keeping it [[18]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil-aristotle-life-is-maintenance-of-heat).
To live is to be warm and moist, while old age and the corpse are dry and cold
[[19]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-longitudine-to-live-is-to-be-warm-and-moist). Both definitions run through the next two thousand years.

> "by life we mean self-sustained nutrition, growth, and decay." (ζωὴν δὲ λέγομεν τὴν δι’ αὑτοῦ τροφήν τε καὶ
> αὔξησιν καὶ φθίσιν.) [[16]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-deanima-life-is-self-nourishment-growth-decay)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTjcdeEm3cWUjzPEEW

> "BIRTH, then, is the original suffusion of the nutritive soul with heat, and life is the maintenance of this
> heat." [[18]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#wil-aristotle-life-is-maintenance-of-heat) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhCV8opeqevMf7Pbdse

**Elsewhere.** Around the same time, Zhuangzi defined life by position, not by activity: human life is qi
gathered [[20]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-zhuangzi-life-gathering-of-qi). "When it gathers, there is life; when it disperses, there is
death." [[20]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-zhuangzi-life-gathering-of-qi) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiiqyDOxIbrfG74vX80. In the early
centuries CE, Caraka defined āyus (life, lifespan) as a union of body, senses, mind and self
[[21]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-caraka-ayus-union-definition). Neither makes life a stuff: in both, it is a state or a relation
[[22]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-asia-life-is-a-state-not-a-stuff).

**Against this:** [[23]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-entelechy-is-not-an-agent). For Aristotle the soul is the first entelechy of an
organic body, not an agent added to it [[24]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-deanima-soul-first-entelechy-organic-body), so reading him as the
ancestor of a "vital force" is wrong.

## 3. Life becomes a gift: the life-giving Spirit (c. 55 – 426 CE)

**Before → after.** Before this, life was something a body has or does. Christianity made the decisive kind of
life something given, by a giver who *makes alive*. Paul sets the first Adam, made "a living being" (ψυχὴν
ζῶσαν), against the last Adam, made "a life-giving spirit" (πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν), and he puts the psychic first and
the spiritual after [[25]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-1cor15-psyche-zosa-pneuma-zoopoioun). John's Jesus comes so that people "may have
life, and that they may have it more abundantly" [[26]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-john-10-10-zoe-perisson). The Creed of 381 calls the Holy Spirit τὸ
ζωοποιόν, *vivificantem*, the life-maker [[27]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-nicene-spirit-zoopoion-vivificantem). Augustine reads Paul's
pair as two states of one body: now an animal body, at the resurrection a life-giving spirit
[[28]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-augustine-animal-body-to-life-giving-spirit). The contrast lasted. In 1737 Lampe writes that giving life is a
far greater thing than merely living [[29]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-lampe-living-soul-vs-life-giving-spirit).

> Ἐγένετο ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος Ἀδὰμ εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν· ὁ ἔσχατος Ἀδὰμ εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν. ("The last Adam became
> a life-giving spirit.") [[25]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-1cor15-psyche-zosa-pneuma-zoopoioun) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhK94vxWCagGA89OB80

> "And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life" (καὶ εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, τὸ κύριον, τὸ ζωοποιὸν)
> [[27]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-nicene-spirit-zoopoion-vivificantem) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhIhQ6LBhsIxC1NROln

> "I have come that they may have life, and that they may have it more abundantly."
> [[26]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-john-10-10-zoe-perisson) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTr3wynYIzqNBBuj0p

**Against this:** [[10]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-heb-breath-or-spirit-is-the-translators-choice). The Greek Psalter uses one word,
πνεῦμα, both for the creatures' life that God withdraws and for the Spirit he sends
[[30]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-psalm104-lxx-one-pneuma-two-englishes). The clean line between "life" and "the life-giver" is partly
drawn by translators.

## 4. The lamp: innate heat burning radical moisture (c. 1250 – 1647)

**Before → after.** Galen made breathing the guard of the innate heat [[31]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-galen-respiration-guards-innate-heat).
Medieval Latin medicine turned that heat into a lamp with a fixed supply of oil. Two things changed: ageing got
a mechanism, and so longevity got a programme. Roger Bacon says natural heat lives in natural moisture and is fed
by it, yet slowly consumes it, "and thus it is the cause of extinguishing itself"
[[32]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-bacon-heat-consumes-its-own-oil). Pietro d'Abano places the innate heat in the "radical moisture" like a
form in matter [[33]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-abano-innate-heat-in-radical-moisture-as-form-in-matter). The *De secretis mulierum* says
that once this moisture is consumed, no medicine helps [[34]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-secretis-life-resides-in-radical-moisture). If life
is a lamp, it can be tended. The *Regimen senum* printed under Arnald says the accidents of old age can be
removed or slowed [[35]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-arnald-old-age-can-be-retarded), and Bacon holds that a great prolongation of life is
possible [[36]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-bacon-great-prolongation-possible). The picture held into the 17th century. Varchi reports that
many simply called natural heat "life" [[37]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-varchi-natural-heat-called-life). Burggrav (1610) describes a lamp
made from a man's blood that burns as long as he lives [[38]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/alchemy-medicine#alch-burggrav-lamp-of-life-from-blood).

> "natural heat gradually, successively, and accidentally dissolves and consumes it, and thus it is the cause of
> extinguishing itself" [[32]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-bacon-heat-consumes-its-own-oil) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bh9LDVEzhKX1hIfaQVm

> "the natural heat lasts as long as the radical moisture lasts, from which it feeds and nourishes itself
> continuously, not otherwise than the flame of oil" [[37]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-varchi-natural-heat-called-life)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhIGEvL1WSshESOG26Q

> "firmiter tenemus quod hec magna prolongatio vite possibilis est et potest fieri certis modis." (Our English: we firmly
> hold that this great prolongation of life is possible and can be done in certain ways.)
> [[36]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-bacon-great-prolongation-possible) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bh9LDVEzhKX1hIfaQXK

**The seat of life, sought by hand.** In the same centuries, a philosophical novel stages the search for where
life lives as an experiment. Ibn Tufayl's Hayy (c. 1175), raised by a doe, opens her chest with stones when she
dies, to find the seat of the harm. In the heart he finds two cavities, the right full of clotted blood and the
left "empty, containing nothing" [[39]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-opens-the-doe-seeking-the-seat). What he sought had been there
and left; the body was only its tool [[40]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-what-left-was-the-mother). Then he opens the left cavity of a
living animal and finds a burning white vapour, and the animal dies at once
[[41]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-vivisection-hot-vapour-moved-animal). Through that one spirit, every animal is one
[[42]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-animal-one-through-its-spirit). The lamp gave life a fuel. Hayy gives it an address: one place in
the body, a hot vapour that can leave whole. That is the frame Harvey's blood and Descartes's clock would
contest [[43]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-harvey-life-resides-in-blood) [[44]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-death-body-decays-not-soul-leaves).

> "He saw that void space full of a vaporous air, like a white mist. He inserted his finger into it and found it
> to be so hot that it burned him, and that animal died on the spot. So it became clear to him that this moist
> vapor was what had moved this animal" [[41]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#wil2-hayy-vivisection-hot-vapour-moved-animal)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BijWMYoRxgM52PNK0RV

**Against this:** [[45]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-med-heat-moisture-is-instrument-not-definition). In the same texts heat and moisture
are the soul's instrument, and Avicenna lists life, innate heat and spirit as three separate gifts of the heart
[[46]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-avicenna-heart-gives-life-heat-spirit). In the same century, Aquinas defined the living by self-motion
[[15]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/medieval#med-aquinas-living-things-move-themselves).

## 5. The living cosmos becomes a working programme (1482 – 1620)

**Before → after.** That the cosmos is a living creature was an ancient thesis. The *Timaeus* says so
[[47]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-timaeus-cosmos-zoon-empsychon-ennoun), and the *Hermetica* says nothing in the cosmos is dead
[[48]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-hermetica-cosmos-pleroma-of-life-nothing-dead). It was also contested: Lucretius said the sky lacks vital
motion and sense [[49]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-lucretius-world-lacks-vital-motion). What changed in the Renaissance is that the world's
life became something one could *use*. Ficino says the world-spirit is animated like any animal, and that by
applying our spirit to it through art, celestial goods pass into us [[50]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-ficino-world-animated-spirit-applied).
He sends the old to live among green plants, which breathe out to increase man's spirit
[[51]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-ficino-green-plants-breathe-into-spirit). Agrippa calls it absurd that flies and worms should live while
the world does not [[52]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-agrippa-absurd-that-world-not-live). Gilbert (1600) argues the same way from the
magnet [[53]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-gilbert-soulless-stars-below-the-worm), and Campanella says the whole world feels
[[54]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-campanella-whole-world-feels).

> "That this is animated, just as any animal is, and much more effectively, is proven not only by Platonic
> arguments but also by the testimonies of the Arab astrologers." [[50]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-ficino-world-animated-spirit-applied)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BfLPSiUU6Nn085Z3oxV

> "Pitiable is the state of the stars, abject the lot of earth, if this high dignity of soul is denied them,
> while it is granted to the worm, the ant, the roach, to plants and morels"
> [[53]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-gilbert-soulless-stars-below-the-worm) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bem5dVhQBjrpvuayx9s

> "Let them frequently spend time among green and sweet-smelling plants. For these, being living and breathing,
> breathe forth their essence to increase the spirit  of man." [[51]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-ficino-green-plants-breathe-into-spirit)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeiybVV2XaXMYfWtoC2

**Against this:** [[55]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-ren-panpsychism-not-one-world-soul). Patrizi, Gilbert and Campanella give grounds that
exclude each other, and Campanella denies that the world soul is the operator at all
[[56]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/renaissance#ren-campanella-sense-not-from-world-soul). Behind it stands [[57]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-anc-living-world-was-contested): the
living world was always one party in a debate.

## 6. The body becomes a machine, and its critics name "dead matter" (1633 – 1748)

**Before → after.** Before, the soul gave the body its heat and motion. Descartes calls that an error
[[58]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-error-soul-gives-heat-motion). He asks readers to consider the body as a machine made by God's
hands [[59]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-body-machine). Death, for him, is not the soul leaving but a principal part of the body
decaying, as a clock runs down [[44]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-death-body-decays-not-soul-leaves). Hobbes (1651) concludes that
life "is but a motion of Limbs" and asks why automata should not have an artificial life
[[60]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-hobbes-life-is-motion-of-limbs). The words for the matter left over came from the other side. More calls
matter "stupid" [[61]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-more-matter-stupid), Conway asks what progress "dead matter" could ever make
[[62]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-conway-dead-matter-never-better), and Law calls it "dead Materiality" [[63]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-law-dead-materiality). By
1748 La Mettrie defends the philosophers "who looked upon animals as machines" against their mockers
[[64]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-lamettrie-reparation-descartes). Organisation, he says, suffices for everything
[[65]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-lamettrie-organisation-suffices), and his evidence is life that will not leave the parts: flesh that
palpitates after death, a cut-out heart that beats again when pricked, a polyp cut into pieces that become as
many animals [[66]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-lamettrie-flesh-palpitates-after-death) [[67]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-lamettrie-polyps-against-generation-systems).
Each fibre moves "by a principle that is proper to it" [[68]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-lamettrie-each-fibre-own-principle). The machine
has made life smaller and more widely spread, not removed it.

**Spinoza's way out.** Between the machine and its critics, Spinoza (1677) changed the question. Every thing,
"as far as it lies within itself, strives to persevere in its being" [[69]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-spinoza-each-thing-strives-to-persevere),
and that striving is "nothing but the actual essence of the thing itself" [[70]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-spinoza-conatus-is-actual-essence).
Self-preservation, the old mark of the living (the lamp tended against its own going out), becomes the mark of
being as such. It involves "no finite time": nothing wears out from within, and death always comes from outside
[[71]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-spinoza-conatus-indefinite-duration). That breaks the lamp's account of ageing. (Our reading, not yet a claim: later
definitions of the organism by self-maintenance keep Spinoza's formula and put back the line between living and
non-living that he removed.)

> "Unaquæque res, quantum in se est, in suo esse perseverare conatur." ("Each thing, as far as it lies within
> itself, strives to persevere in its being.") [[69]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil2-spinoza-each-thing-strives-to-persevere)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BembIQgFKlHjuxOPOL7

> "will consider this body as a machine, which, having been made by the hands of God, is incomparably better
> ordered" [[59]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-body-machine) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhIfRgkkd7WhVomjJYS

> "For seeing life is but a motion of Limbs, the beginning whereof is in some principall part within; why may we
> not say, that all Automata (Engines that move themselves by springs and wheeles as doth a watch) have an
> artificiall life?" [[60]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-hobbes-life-is-motion-of-limbs) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOdkuOeBegxKcukcZj

> "after it has undergone infinite changes of motion and figure , it is always compelled to remain exactly as it
> was before: dead." [[62]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-conway-dead-matter-never-better) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BejnthLMr5D66QIHzyM

**Against this:** [[72]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-vit-dead-matter-is-the-critics-word). Descartes says "machine", not "dead matter".
Also [[73]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-ems-motion-is-life-on-both-sides): Hobbes and Cavendish give the same definition of life, motion.
For Cavendish, motion is the life and soul of Nature [[74]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-cavendish-motion-life-and-soul-of-nature). What they
disagree about is whether matter moves itself.

## 7. Life against death: the vitalist definition, and the death of its word (1790 – 1904)

**Before → after.** After the machine, life had to be defined against it. Kant (1790) says an organized being
is not merely a machine, because it has a formative power in itself [[75]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil-kant-organism-formative-power-not-machine).
He reports Blumenbach's view that it is contrary to reason for life to arise from the lifeless
[[76]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-kant-blumenbach-lifeless). Bichat (1800) gives the definition the century kept: life is the sum of the
functions that resist death [[77]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-bichat-1800-ensemble-des-fonctions). He also makes it a ratio between outer
forces and inner resistance [[78]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-bichat-1800-measure-of-life). The force had names: Lebenskraft, and in
Hahnemann's *Organon* (1833) a "Dynamis" that enlivens the body [[79]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-hahnemann-1833-dynamis-organism-unity).
In 1868 Huxley mocked the word: "vitality" has no better status than "aquosity" [[80]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-huxley-1868-vitality-aquosity).
In the same lecture, though, he described living matter by "continual death" [[81]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-huxley-1868-continual-death).
The critics killed the word and kept Bichat's definition [[82]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-vit-killed-word-kept-definition). By 1884 du Prel
calls Lebenskraft "verpönt" (frowned upon) in science [[83]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-duprel-1884-lebenskraft-revives). In 1904 Steiner
says speaking of it had lately been the mark of an unscientific mind [[84]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-steiner-lebenskraft-unscientific-note-1904).

> "la vie est l’ensemble des fonctions qui résistent à la mort." (Our English: life is the sum of the functions that resist
> death.) [[77]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-bichat-1800-ensemble-des-fonctions) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BnEPCQTeRinK2nLUE8d

> "What better philosophical status has “vitality” than “aquosity”?" [[80]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-huxley-1868-vitality-aquosity)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhPYrf7NrmyoyHL7LU9

> "in consequence of that continual death which is the condition of its manifesting vitality"
> [[81]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-huxley-1868-continual-death) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhPYrf7NrmyoyHL7LU7

**The question turned on the machine (1872).** Hobbes had asked whether automata have "an artificiall life"
[[60]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-hobbes-life-is-motion-of-limbs): the machine as a model of the animal. Samuel Butler's *Erewhon* asks the
reverse, whether machines could *become* alive. "The Book of the Machines", an Erewhonian treatise inside the
satire, runs the old marks of life against the steam engine. It must be fed and burns its food "even as man
consumes it", breathes air, has "a pulse and circulation" [[85]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-butler-vapour-engine-feeds). Its little
consciousness now is no security, for "A mollusc has not much consciousness"
[[86]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-butler-mechanical-consciousness). And it reproduces through us, as the clover through the bee
[[87]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-butler-man-in-machine-reproduction). It is the first text on our pages to ask the question now asked of
AI. It is satire and reported speech, so it must be quoted as the treatise's, not as Butler's view.

> "But who can say that the vapour engine has not a kind of consciousness? Where does consciousness begin, and
> where end? Who can draw the line? Who can draw any line?" [[86]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-butler-mechanical-consciousness)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BllvN0GOgj17qBVAmLq

**Against this:** [[88]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-vit-binary-retrospective). The main figures refuse both sides of the "mechanism versus
vitalism" split. Kant's Blumenbach leaves mechanism a share, and Bergson accepts only vitalism's negative claim.

## 8. Naturphilosophie: the organism as a process, the Earth as alive (1790 – 1851)

**Before → after.** The Romantics did not put a force inside the organism. They made the organism an ongoing
process, and they extended that process to nature as a whole. Goethe (1790) explains all the organs of the
flowering plant from one organ, the leaf [[89]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-goethe-1790-all-organs-from-leaf). Schelling (1798) rejects both
a magical Lebenskraft and "dead" chemical forces [[90]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-schelling-1798-neither-magic-nor-dead). In 1799 he defines
the organism's existence as "not a state of being, but a constant state of being reproduced" [[91]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-schelling-1799-organism-constant-reproduction).
Life arises "against the will of external nature" [[92]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-schelling-1799-life-against-external-nature). One
principle links the inorganic and organic worlds into a universal organism, the old world soul
[[93]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-schelling-1798-world-soul-universal-organism). Fechner takes this furthest. In 1848 he says the moderns
left nature "entseelt", soulless [[94]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-fechner-nanna-nature-left-soulless). In 1851 he makes the Earth a living
being in a higher sense than we are [[95]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-fechner-1851-earth-more-alive-than-we), and he tells the modern story
as soul giving way to Lebenskraft, and Lebenskraft to mechanical force
[[96]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-fechner-1851-separation-soul-lebenskraft-mechanical).

> "Nun besteht aber das Wesen alles Organismus darinn, dafs er keine absolute Thätigkeit sey, (dergleichen z. B.
> mit dem Begriff der Lebenskraft gedacht wird, sondern eine durch Receptivität vermittelte Thätigkeit, denn das
> Bestehen des Organismus ist nicht ein Seyn, sondern ein beständiges Reproducirtwerden."
> [[91]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-schelling-1799-organism-constant-reproduction) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhrcT8DgSOh6NMWzoXr

> "the Earth appear as a living, more independent, more individually distinct being in a higher sense than we are
> ourselves, whereas our own life falls far short in fullness and depth"
> [[95]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-fechner-1851-earth-more-alive-than-we) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOcWNrl434So9ln7JC

> "then, finally, the vital force is also stripped away from it, and at last, everything is done by mechanical
> force ." [[96]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-fechner-1851-separation-soul-lebenskraft-mechanical) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOcWNrl434So9ln7ET

**Against this:** [[97]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-rom-naturphilosophie-not-lebenskraft-vitalism). This is not "vital force" vitalism:
Schelling defines the organism *against* Lebenskraft. Also [[98]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-rom-living-earth-not-shared): only Fechner
makes the Earth a living subject, while Hegel calls it "das allgemeine Bild des Lebens", the universal image of life [[99]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-hegel-1817-earth-geological-organism).

## 9. Life as movement, will and lived experience: Bergson and Lebensphilosophie (1873 – 1929)

**Before → after.** The question moved from the living body to life as it is lived and valued. Nietzsche
(1873–76) judges history by whether it serves life [[100]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil-nietzsche-serve-history-not-life). William James (1902)
endorses the view that the end of religion is "not God, but life, more life" [[101]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-james-more-life-end-of-religion-1902).
Dilthey (1906) narrows Erlebnis to the moments that open up for the poet a trait of life
[[102]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil-dilthey-erlebnis-unlocks-life). Bergson (1907) defines life as a movement, with materiality as the inverse
movement [[103]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil-bergson-life-is-movement), and as "a tendency to act upon brute matter"
[[104]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-bergson-life-tendency-to-act-on-matter-1907). His élan vital is finite, given once and for all
[[105]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-bergson-elan-finite). Whitehead (1929) calls life "a bid for freedom" [[106]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil-whitehead-life-bid-for-freedom).

> "En réalité la vie est un mouvement, la matérialité est le mouvement inverse, et chacun de ces deux mouvements
> est simple" [[103]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil-bergson-life-is-movement) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhCv2viZJV7K296uaVF

> "Mais l'élan est fini, et il a été donné une fois pour toutes." [[105]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-bergson-elan-finite)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhCv2viZJV7K296uaVK

> "so dienen sie der Historie, aber nicht dem Leben, und sind todt, bevor sie gestorben sind" (Our English: they
> serve history, but not life, and are dead before they have died.) [[100]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil-nietzsche-serve-history-not-life)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhCtYVjiuPPRgFqrsRH

**Against this:** [[107]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-wil-zoe-and-bios-conflated). Schopenhauer, Nietzsche and Dilthey define life as lived
(bios, Erleben), not the living body (zōē). Putting them in one series with Aristotle joins two different
questions.

## 10. Aliveness becomes a felt quality (1881 – 1910)

**Before → after.** The English noun "aliveness", for a condition one feels, appears on our pages through New
Thought, the American mind-cure movement. It turns life into a sensation that comes in degrees and can be raised
by will. Evans (1881) had already made all life a force and all force a manifestation of primal Life
[[108]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-evans-life-spiritual-force-not-fluid-1881). Helen Wilmans (1898) gives the earliest use we hold: aliveness
as a felt condition of her own childhood [[109]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-wilmans-aliveness-childhood-1898). Troward (1904) makes
"livingness" a matter of degree [[110]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-troward-livingness-degrees-1904). In 1910 he makes the "feeling of
aliveness" the first state of Spirit [[111]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-troward-spirit-feeling-of-aliveness-1910). Atkinson, writing as "Yogi
Ramacharaka", tells readers to rub their hands until they feel "aliveness" [[112]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-ramacharaka-hands-aliveness-1906).
William James (1906–7) gives the same experience a psychologist's form, and is the bridge from
vitality to felt aliveness. "Everyone is familiar with the phenomenon of feeling more or less alive on different
days," and "compared with what we ought to be, we are only half awake" [[113]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-james-feeling-more-or-less-alive).
Second wind shows "stored-up reserves of energy that are ordinarily not called upon"
[[114]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-james-second-wind-reserves), and "Excitements, ideas, and efforts … are what carry us over the dam"
[[115]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-james-excitements-ideas-efforts). His language is still the furnace's ("Our fires are damped, our drafts
are checked"), but the furnace is now felt from inside, and it can be raised. In the same year Bergson makes all
life an effort to store energy and release it [[116]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#wil2-bergson-life-store-and-spend-energy). Scheler then makes
"ascending" and "descending" life a feeling with its own values [[117]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-scheler-vital-values-noble-common).

> "Everyone is familiar with the phenomenon of feeling more or less alive on different days."
> [[113]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#wil2-james-feeling-more-or-less-alive) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhdQl2RhMNETOGon2Wq

Atkinson, again as Ramacharaka, in 1905 glosses prāṇa as "Absolute Energy" [[118]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-ramacharaka-prana-absolute-energy), where the
Haṭhayogapradīpikā's own commentary says prāṇa is vāyu, wind [[119]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-prana-hyp-vayu). Here the comparative strand
turns: from about 1905 Asian breath-words reach English as "energy" [[120]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-asia-energy-gloss-has-a-date).

> "The aptest word I can apply to myself as a child is "aliveness." I was — in my own way — tremendously alive."
> [[109]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-wilmans-aliveness-childhood-1898) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BnODiz16K6rCesCHmwQ

> "Rub the hands to-gether briskly for a few minutes, and then swing them to-and-fro a little while, until they
> have that undefinable feeling of "aliveness" and be-ing full of Energy." [[112]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/modern#mod-ramacharaka-hands-aliveness-1906)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgQro6KhYX2AEbzkloy

> "we, in this work, will speak of the principle as “Prana,” this word being the Sanskrit term meaning “Absolute
> Energy.”" [[118]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-ramacharaka-prana-absolute-energy) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgQrmvo8gdwpMlkge7J

**Against this:** [[121]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-mod-aliveness-is-a-new-thought-word). A history organised around "aliveness" risks
reading every tradition through mind-cure's assumption that life is a felt, gradable quality one can cultivate.
This page is exposed to that risk too.
