## D. The split: how "soul" and "life" came apart (1637–1720)

**Before.** For Aristotle and the schools, to be alive was to have at least the nutritive soul. Life was what a
soul does. Breathing, digestion, growth and the heartbeat were all works of soul.

**The turning point: Descartes.** Descartes keeps only the rational soul and hands everything else to the
body's machinery. In *Discours* V (1637) he finds in the body "precisely all those which may exist in us
independently of all power of thinking, and consequently without being in any measure owing to the soul". To run
them he needs no "vegetative or sensitive soul, beyond kindling in the heart one of those fires without light"
[[71]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#soul-wd-descartes-functions-without-soul) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bem5RoRnUr0TFVAeab1. By the *Passions*
(1649) the old view has become an error: "That it is an error to believe the soul gives motion and heat to the
body" (*Erroneum esse credere animam dare motum & calorem corpori*) [[72]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-error-soul-gives-heat-motion)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhI8fARDfzZd3a9A690. Death is now a broken machine, not a departing soul: the living
body differs from the dead "as a clock or other automaton" [[73]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-death-body-decays-not-soul-leaves)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhI8fARDfzZd3a9A691. Of the old soul, "il ne reste rien en nous que nous devions
attribuer à nostre ame, sinon nos pensées" [[74]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-soul-left-with-thoughts). Animals have no soul at all:
"it is Nature that acts in them according to the disposition of their organs: Just as one sees that a clock…"
[[75]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-nature-acts-organs) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhIfRgkkd7WhVomjJYV.

**After.** "Soul" now means mind, and "life" needs a new name or none. The replies try to put life back into
nature without putting a mind in every leaf:

- **Henry More (1659):** "Matter is stupid, or destitute of vital Sympathy and Coactivity, Spirit must be vital"
  [[76]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-more-matter-stupid) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BejWIDHvgIoRz3OeuEo. Hence his Spirit of Nature, a soul
  "without Sense and Animadversion" [[41]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#soul-wo-more-spirit-of-nature-defined).
- **Cudworth (1678):** plastic nature is a life without consciousness, "The Plastick and Vegetative Life of Nature
  the Lowest of all Lives, and Inferiour to the Sensitive" and "forasmuch as the Plastick Nature is a Life, it
  must needs be Incorporeal" [[77]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#wil-cudworth-plastic-nature-is-a-life) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BejVn7KJPQwQ47iFcNq.
  Its energy is "a certain Drowsie, Unawakened, or Astonish'd Cogitation" [[78]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-cudworth-vital-energy-not-local-motion).
  Aristotle's vegetative soul returns under another name.
- **Margaret Cavendish (1664–66):** she abolishes the soulless part instead. "Nature is a self-moving, and
  consequently a self-living and self-knowing infinite body" [[79]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-cavendish-nature-self-living-self-knowing)
  https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOa4UEhGb55GDaCLa5. "all parts or degrees of Matter are living and knowing, but not
  all are self-moving" [[80]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-cavendish-all-matter-living-not-all-self-moving) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOa4UEhGb55GDaCLeF.
  "Motion is the life and soul of Nature" [[81]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-cavendish-motion-life-and-soul-of-nature).
- **Leibniz (1714):** he accepts the machine and multiplies the souls. "the machines of nature, namely, living
  bodies, are still machines in their smallest parts ad infinitum" [[82]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-leibniz-machines-in-smallest-parts)
  https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeosOWpUn6vqZzdq14b. And "each living body has a dominant entelechy, which in an
  animal is the soul; but the members of this living body are full of other living beings, plants, animals"
  [[83]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#soul-wd-leibniz-dominant-entelechy-is-soul) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeosOWpUn6vqZzdq14e. Aristotle's word
  *entelechy* is back.
- **Stahl (c. 1700–1709):** for Stahl the soul itself rules the body's vital motions. Our page has the Stahlian
  energy "certainly inherent in the LIVING body—indeed, it is what makes the body living" (*imò hoc tale reddens,
  ENERGIA*) [[84]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#soul-wd-stahl-immanent-energy-makes-living) ◐ *(medium: the word anima is not on that page)*
  https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhNfV24qX5DMNDLwPzz. His opponents report the doctrine plainly: "The Stahlian
  physicians say that the soul drives the blood about so violently…" [[85]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-kruger-1758-stahlians-soul-drives-blood)
  https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhboDgy9F13HYalE44G. Maine de Biran's verdict is that Stahl "transports" the conscious
  soul to "the organic or purely vital functions" [[86]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-biran-stahl-soul-transported).

**What came of it.**
- **Life detached from soul.** By 1758 movement is explained by irritability, "a property of the matter of the
  animal body, for which no sensation is required" [[87]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/vitalism#vit-kruger-1758-irritability-dismisses-soul).
- **"Vital force" took the soul's old work** (see essay 1, the lexicon).
- **Fechner (1851) tells the story as three stripping-aways:** "the body now also scorns the soul … and says: 'My
  vital force will do just as well'; then, finally, the vital force is also stripped away from it, and at last,
  everything is done by mechanical force" [[88]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-fechner-1851-separation-soul-lebenskraft-mechanical)
  https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOcWNrl434So9ln7ET. In *Nanna* (1848) the spirit has risen out of nature and "sie entseelt zurückgelassen hat" (left
  it soulless) [[89]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/romantic-naturphilosophie#rom-fechner-nanna-nature-left-soulless)
  https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOcWgAfDFur4esBIQQ.

**Critique.**
- **The split was neither sudden nor total.** Gassendi and Willis kept a corporeal, fiery soul for animals ("the
  soul is therefore a certain little flame… As long as this flame thrives… the animal lives")
  [[90]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-gassendi-soul-little-flame-willis) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bh9MpeDWI2wky57PpQk.
- **Life and soul had also come apart before Descartes.** Galen already assigned growth to nature, not soul
  [[91]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/ancient#anc-galen-nf-growth-is-work-of-nature-not-soul), and the Stoics graded physis below psychē.
- **What Descartes changed** was to make the line between the soul and everything else the line between mind and
  machine.

---

## Open questions

- **The Coimbra commentary (Conimbricenses, *In tres libros De anima*, 1598).** It is not on SL. It is the textbook
  form of the ladder that Descartes was taught at La Flèche.
- **Stahl's *Theoria medica vera* (1708).** It is not found on SL, so the "anima rules the body" line has no page in
  his own words yet.
- **Chinese and Indic ladders of living things.** Do Xunzi's grades (water and fire have qi, plants have life,
  animals have awareness, humans have yi) belong beside Aristotle's? This thread has no claim on them yet.

title: 5. Life beyond Europe: ik', tonalli, cama, mauri, ẹ̀mí, niya, sěmangat
md:
**The question.** Pages 1–4 answer "what makes a thing alive?" mostly from Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic, Sanskrit
and Chinese. This page asks the same three questions of the Americas, Africa, Oceania and island Asia. What makes a
thing alive? Where does its life sit? And what did people do to keep life, or to bring it back?

**How to read it.** ✓ means the claim is verified on a Source Library page. ○ means scholarly background that SL
does not hold. Such a claim is `unverified` in the KB and is given here only for orientation. Quotes are SL's English
(a model translation of the page) unless the original is given. Every claim on this page is tagged `thread:world`,
and its native word is tagged `term:<word>`. The soul half of the same
material (wairua, pixan, the Nahua dead, plural souls) is in the soul concept, in its world claims and
its essay on many souls.

**Whose voice.** Every claim is tagged `voice:insider` or `voice:outsider`. Insider means a text by people of the
tradition: the Popol Vuh, the Ritual of the Bacabs, the Nahuatl column of the Florentine Codex, Grey's karakia,
Eastman, the Tibetan liturgy. Outsider means an ethnographer or a missionary: Best, Tregear, Farrow, Ellis, Spencer and
Gillen, Skeat, and the friars' dictionaries (Motul, Pío Pérez, Molina, Santo Tomás, Crowther). Of the 27 life claims,
12 rest on an insider voice and 15 on an outsider one. The split runs by tradition, as the aliveness atlas predicted.
The Maya and Nahua material is mostly insider, because both peoples wrote their own books in the Latin alphabet
within a generation of the conquest. Oceania and Africa are almost all outsider: on SL, their words reach us through
colonial ethnographers.

---

## A. Maya: life is made, it breathes, and it greens again

**Making people.** The Popol Vuh, a K'iche' text, tells how the gods made people in four tries. The first animals
cannot speak. The mud body "was soft, compressed, and limp; it simply crumbled and became wet." The wooden people
speak and multiply. But "they turned out foolish, without hearts and without understanding. And so they did not
remember their creator anymore" [[5]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-maya-popol-vuh-four-tries) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bn0a1fFYMTCEUIROCi6.
The K'iche' on the facing scan is *macu habi quigux mapu habi qui- naoh*. They had no k'u'x (heart) and no na'oj
(knowing) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bn0a1fFYMTCEUIROCi7. The people who finally live are made of food: "Only
yellow corn and white corn were their flesh; only food became the arms and legs of the men"
[[6]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-maya-popol-vuh-maize-flesh) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bn0a1fFYMTCEUIROCj3. Life here is no breath blown
into clay, as in Genesis 2:7 [[7]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-gen27-nishmat-hayyim-nefesh-hayyah). It is the right *substance*, ground and
mixed, plus a heart that remembers its makers. (See page 3, §5.)

**Breath and wind.** Pío Pérez's dictionary runs one chain for ik/ikal: "wind, air, breath, breathing, spirit,
life" [[8]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-maya-perez-ik-wind-breath-life) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BorY6q8Y4nDFmJz5kgP. "Spirit" at the
end of the chain is the friar's Spanish *espíritu*, so the claim is tagged `friar-gloss`. In the Classic
inscriptions, death is "his white breath withered", *k'a'ay u sak ik'il* ○ [unverified].
That is Houston, Stuart and Taube's reading; SL does not hold the inscriptions.

**Greening again.** *Cuxtal* is "life, living, alive", and the verb means "to live; for plants to grow green again
… To recover from serious illness" [[9]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-maya-perez-cuxtal-life-regreening)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BorY6q8Y4nDFmJz5keu. To live is to green again and to get well.

**What people did.** The Ritual of the Bacabs, an insider book of curing, treats illnesses as winds to be named,
seized and cast down. The patient is cured "with the wind of the fan". SL's English renders *u yikal nicte*, "the
wind of the plumeria", as "the erotic wind-seizure" [[10]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-maya-bacabs-wind-of-disease)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bp0Oylev5p16rMkC1IQ. That rendering is tagged `mistranslation`.

## B. Nahua: life is a brief warmth, sent from the sky

**Warmth.** The Nahuatl funeral address in Florentine Codex Book III says *ca çan titotonioa*: "it is only for a
tiny moment, only for a brief instant, that we merely warm ourselves" [[11]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-nahua-life-is-warming-oneself)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiWncq5L5vvO8hZT9iQ.

**The tonalli.** Book X says the *tonalli* comes from Ometecuhtli's twelfth heaven. When a child is conceived, its
tonalli "enters within it; Ometecuhtli sends it" (*imjtic calaquj: qujoalioa in vme te cutli*)
[[12]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-nahua-tonalli-sent-into-womb) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiWnd8DToPCDrACqSey. Sahagún's Spanish column
makes it "la influencia y calor": an astrological heat, not "ánima". Molina's dictionary defines *tonalli* as
"calor del sol, o tiempo de estío" (the heat of the sun, or the dry season), and lists *tonalcaualtia*, "to be
frightened" [[13]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-nahua-molina-tonalli-sun-heat-fright) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bnem43lrVBrNps0Cw8r. Heat,
day-sign and fright are one word family. That is why later scholarship reads soul loss through fright as a loss of
tonalli ○ (Soul [unverified]).

**Breath that speaks.** *Ihijo, itlatol*, "his breath, his word", is said of rulers' speech: "the revered breath,
the revered word of our lord" [[14]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-nahua-ihiyotl-breath-is-word) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiWnd2AlZa6bx0drODP.
Elsewhere SL's English turns *oyhjiotl ticmomachiti* into "you have endured the breath of life". It is an idiom of
weariness, and "of life" is the translator's addition (tagged `mistranslation`).

**What people did.** People strengthened a child's tonalli by bathing and naming it on a good day sign. They put a
greenstone in the mouth of the dead "and it is said that it becomes their heart". They fed the dead for four
years (Soul [[1]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-nahua-greenstone-becomes-heart), `world-nahua-mictlan-dog-four-years`). The tonalli cures of
Ruiz de Alarcón (1629) are not held.

## C. Andean: cama, to give soul, life and being

Inca Garcilaso (1609), son of an Inca noblewoman, explains: "*Pacha Cámac* means he who does with the universe what
the soul does with the body. … *cama* is to give soul, life, being, and substance" [[15]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-andes-cama-give-soul-life-being)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BineOlSwzF08ErsUG3l. Garcilaso is an insider, but he writes in Spanish and frames the
idea scholastically: "what the soul does with the body" is Aristotle's form. The friar Santo Tomás (1560) spreads
one Christian "alma, por la qual viuimos" over three Quechua words: *camaquencu*, *songo* (heart) and *çamaynin*
(breath) [[16]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-andes-santotomas-alma-camaquen-songo-samay) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BnepwfeWuAaK2OMdmRn. The
animating power, the heart and the breath were three different things that the dictionary folded into one. The
main insider source on *camaquen* and the huacas, the Huarochirí manuscript, is not held. Nor is González
Holguín's 1608 *Vocabulario*.

## D. Māori: mauri, hau, and the life of a forest

**Life is plural and has a place.** Best (1900) separates three things at death: "The wairua lives on afte death
of a person, but the mauri or spark of life is extinct, and thi manawa ora or breath of life has departed for all
time" [[17]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/oceania#world-maori-best-mauri-spark-manawa-ora) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bp0CyatFNROVzglVNWi (SL's OCR
spelling kept). The *hau* belongs to land as well as to people: "the hau of the land, of a forest, of
a tree, of the kumara" [[18]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/oceania#world-maori-best-hau-of-land-forest-kumara) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bp0CyatFNROVzglVNWv.
This is the strongest *world* sense of life on the page. A forest is alive in the way a person is, and it can be
bewitched in the same way.

**Where the forest's life is kept.** "The mauri of a forest or a river is a talisman, and whilst it is in its proper
place it keeps the hau of the forest, stream, or land, so that birds multiply and trees flourish" (Tregear 1904)
[[19]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/oceania#world-maori-tregear-forest-mauri-keeps-hau) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bp0Ata9eMxwcJfdXqop. The right wing of a
kākā, the *kira*, "is the mauri of the forest birds … It is, of course, carefully concealed"
[[20]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/oceania#world-maori-best-kira-mauri-forest-birds) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bp0CyatFNROVzglVNWz.

**What people did.** At the *ahi taitai* fire a priest roasts and eats part of the first bird, and the rest goes to
Tāne. The one insider voice in this section is a food karakia from Grey's collection (1853). It speaks to the crop
directly: "*Koi to mauri ka tupu, Tupu koe e to mauri … Ka te tupu koe i to mauri ora*", and then "*Whangaia nga
atua*", feed the gods [[21]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/oceania#world-maori-grey-karakia-mauri-ora-food) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiX2HcVGGzCYJkE72OG.
A scholar's mauri was guarded by a stone: "Here is my mauri, thy mauri, O Io the Parent!"
[[22]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/oceania#world-maori-best-school-mauri-stone) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bp0B1B7UExD7xtPv47i. This links to mana, the
power such "mana-possessing stones" carry [[23]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/animism-ethnography#anim-codrington-mana-not-physical).

**Flattening.** Best renders mauri "life-principle". SL's model English for Grey's karakia adds "life-force", a
word the Māori text does not contain. Tregear calls the hau "the essence or soul of the land". All are tagged
`mistranslation`. Mauri is the placed, guardable life of a particular thing, not a general force.

## E. Hawaiian: mauli ola and ea

Emerson (1909), annotating a prayer to Pele, says *mauli-ola* "was applied to the breath of life, or to the
physician's power of healing. In the Maori tongue the word mauri, corresponding to mauli, means life, the seat of
life" [[24]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/oceania#world-hawaii-emerson-mauli-ola-breath-of-life) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiX2CM8jMUJXPSa3M94. *Ea*
means breath, life and sovereignty at once ("the life of the land is perpetuated in righteousness") ○
[unverified]. No SL page found prints it. Malo's *Hawaiian Antiquities*, the
insider source, is held but hidden, and its pages are not served, so it is not cited. What people did:
asking the *ʻaumakua*, ancestor-gods fed at coral altars, to "Bring life to us, to all the family" (Soul [[2]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-hawaii-westervelt-aumakua-bring-life)).

## F. Aranda: life comes from a place

In Spencer and Gillen (1899), a child's life does not come from its parents. It comes from an ancestral spirit at a
particular spot, and the child's *churinga* goes back "to the storehouse of the locality from which the spirit child
came" (Soul [[3]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-aranda-spencer-spirit-child-locality), https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgxPtEuoJrGiK89tIQt). Life
is lodged in the land and in a carved object. This is outsider ethnography throughout, and "reincarnation" and
"double" are the ethnographers' categories. Strehlow, who knew Aranda, is not held.

## G. Yoruba: ẹ̀mí, the breath that is lent

Crowther (1852) glosses *Emmí*: "life, breath, spirit, influence.—*Ki Ọlọrun ki ofu ’ọ li ẹmmi gigun*, 'May God
give you a long life!'—*Emmí abata ni imu odò iṣan*, 'The influence of a fountain makes the brook flow'"
[[25]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/africa#world-yoruba-emi-life-breath-crowther) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiX2oWVbQ5xB9cr9bvl. One word covers breath,
the length of a life, and the moving power of water. Farrow (1926) gives the high god's name *Elemi*, "The Owner
of Breath" [[26]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/africa#world-yoruba-elemi-owner-of-breath-farrow) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bjeab2Id6kN1bhmInuF. Life-breath
is the god's, and it is lent. *Àṣẹ* is the power that makes speech come to pass. In the Ifa verse Farrow prints,
Orunmila goes "to receive authority from the Almighty … All that he said came to pass. Ever since then we say,
'It will come to pass!'" [[27]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/africa#world-yoruba-ase-rendered-authority-farrow) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bjeab2Id6kN1bhmInuS.
"Authority" is Farrow's word, and it flattens àṣẹ, as does Farrow's equation of emi with Greek πνεῦμα.
Crowther was Yoruba-born, but his *Vocabulary* is a mission book. It is tagged `missionary-dictionary`, and its
"spirit" is tagged `friar-gloss`.

## H. Dakota and Lakota: visible breath, and the Great Mystery

The Song of the White Buffalo Maiden, sung by the Teton singer Charging Thunder for Densmore (1918), opens
*niya' tanin'yan … mawa'ni ye*: "with visible breath … I am walking" [[28]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-dakota-niya-visible-breath-densmore)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsgzfJFzM8XTtupoo. Eastman (Ohiyesa, 1902), an insider, remembers his grandmother
teaching him that the Great Mystery is "him who looks at you from every creation. In the wind you hear him whisper
to you. He gives his war-whoop in the thunder" [[29]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-dakota-great-mystery-every-creation-eastman)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bjd1ijpGFud2x7pTSzP. "Great Mystery" is Eastman's own English for *Wakan Tanka*; the
word *wakan* is not on the page. What people did: a father "kept" a dead child's spirit in a bundle holding a
lock of its hair, fed until a final feast (Soul [[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-dakota-spirit-keeping-densmore)). Riggs's Dakota
dictionary, Walker's *Sun Dance* and Eastman's *Soul of the Indian* are not held.

## I. Malay, Tibetan: the life that can wander off

Skeat (1900): the meaning of *sěmangat* "covers both 'soul' and 'life' (i.e. not the state of being alive, but the
cause thereof or 'vital principle')" [[30]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/north-inner-asia#world-malay-semangat-soul-and-life-skeat)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlb8FAkF4UX1aNTkD. Rice has one too: the sěmangat padi, the rice-soul, is taken first at harvest.
A sěmangat can wander off, and it is called back like a fowl. The Tibetan *bla* is the same kind of thing: the
Tshe khrid liturgy summons back the *bla tshe* among the declined life-spans [[31]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#asia-bla-tshe-two-renderings). In
both, life is a portable thing. It can be lost, stolen or ransomed, and a specialist can call it home.

---

## What the comparison shows

1. **Life is placed, and it can be lost.** In these traditions life is a thing in a place: maize flesh, a tonalli
   in the head, the mauri hidden in a forest, a spirit-child's rock, a sěmangat the size of a thumb. Because it is
   in a place, it can be stolen (hau through hair or spittle), frightened out (tonalli), or called back (sěmangat,
   bla, the Buryat "invitation"). European regimen tends a fire that burns down (page 3, §1). The care here is
   closer to keeping and recovering a possession.
2. **The world is alive in the same sense as the person.** The hau of a forest and of a man are the same word. So
   are Crowther's ẹ̀mí of a person and of a spring, and the cuxtal of a person and of a plant that greens again. This
   bears on the atlas's finding that most SL passages place life in the world, not the person.
3. **Breath recurs, but it is rarely the whole story.** Ik', ihiyotl, ẹ̀mí, niya, manawa ora and mauli ola all name
   breath. But each sits beside a heat (tonalli), a heart (k'u'x, songo, ọkàn), or a placed principle (mauri,
   camaquen). The European habit of collapsing these into one "soul" or one "life force" is the main thing the
   translations get wrong.
4. **The flattening has three layers.** The friar's dictionary renders the word as the Christian soul. The
   ethnographer renders it as Tylor's "vital principle". SL's model English then adds "life-force" where neither
   wrote it (Grey's karakia; Budge's ka in soul-kb). See [[32]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-cmp-life-force-is-a-gloss-layer).

## Critiques that bear on this page

- **Mostly outsider voices.** 15 of the 27 claims rest on ethnographers and missionaries. The Oceania and Africa
  sections have one insider line each. A reader should take Best's and Farrow's systems as reports, not doctrine.
- **"Reincarnation", "double", "vital principle" and "soul"** are the observers' categories, reused in each other's
  books (Best likens wairua to the Egyptian Ka; Skeat quotes Tylor).
- **The model's English is a third observer.** Where the claim turns on a word, the claim cites the original line.

## Open questions

- **Huarochirí manuscript, Ruiz de Alarcón, Molina's Spanish-Nahuatl, Olmos's *Tratado de hechicerías*.** The last
  two are held but not yet mined. Are there tonalli cures in Olmos?
- **Malo's *Hawaiian Antiquities*** is hidden. Making it readable would give Hawaiian an insider voice.
- **Rattray's *Ashanti*** is held, but only its index surfaced for okra and sunsum. Read the chapter.
- **Kojiki and Nihongi** are held: tama and *iki* (breath, life) from the texts themselves.
- **Not held:** a further 32 works are recorded as not held.
